author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rhode Island’s people, museums and historic sites play a central role in a new NBC 10 News project examining New England’s contribution to the American story ahead of the nation’s 250th anniversary. The series begins with Indigenous history at the Tomaquag Museum and follows the state’s distinctive path toward independence.

The reporting connects Roger Williams’ advocacy of religious liberty with the First Baptist Church in America in Providence. It also revisits the 1772 burning of the British customs schooner Gaspee in Narragansett Bay, an act that came more than a year before the Boston Tea Party.

Rhode Island formally renounced allegiance to King George III on May 4, 1776, two months before the Declaration of Independence. The series also highlights the First Rhode Island Regiment, whose Black, Indigenous and white soldiers fought in the 1778 Battle of Rhode Island.

Additional stops include the Nathanael Greene Homestead in Coventry and the Independent Man atop the State House. Together, the locations show how the state’s history extends beyond a single anniversary: museums, reenactors and preservation groups continue interpreting whose experiences shaped the region and how those stories are passed to new generations.
dek: A regional history project traces Indigenous experience, religious liberty, the Gaspee affair and the First Rhode Island Regiment.
headline: Rhode Island history anchors New England’s America 250 story
